groundTruthNarrative: Cottonwood Prairie's record year is a good outcome, not evidence of good management. Revenue rose 46.5% because grain prices rose 36-46% from February 2026 while bushels handled were flat; handling revenue did not move, the auditor attributes the margin gain to inventory appreciation during the rally, and 22 peers without any new program grew similarly. The Operational Excellence program's only measured effect, the 6% fall in cost per bushel, is entirely the $293K cut in maintenance spending, while the deferred backlog tripled to $1.26M and is concentrated in Harlan Junction dust-control items. The insurer found critical dust hazards there, and a July hot-bearing near-miss on a leg whose bearing replacement had twice been deferred was closed without the investigation policy requires, so its cause is unknown. Staff report hazards readily; the response is what fails. Drying and grading depend on one undocumented 63-year-old superintendent with no successor, though whether his skill, rather than newer dryers, explains his sites' better shrink is unestablished. Whether the expansion is viable is unknown because the proposal is baselined on spike revenue and contains no margin or debt-service analysis. Fix the safety hazards and start succession now; rebuild the expansion case before voting.

answers.rationale: The board and GM credit the program (E1, E5), but bushels handled were flat (E3), handling revenue was flat and the auditor attributes the margin gain to inventory appreciation during the price rally (E2), and 22 peers with no new program had similar revenue (+41% median) and net-savings (+97% median) growth, with Cottonwood mid-pack (E4). The program's one measured effect, 1.0 cent/bushel, is entirely the maintenance cut (E6), about $0.3M against a $5.3M rise in net savings. The evidence counts against the claim, not merely fails to support it.

Grain sales are 91% of revenue; bushels received fell 0.9% (E3) while corn and soybean prices rose 46% and 36% (E4); handling, drying and storage revenue was flat at $9.8-9.9M (E2); peers with flat volume grew revenue by a similar median 41% (E4). Price, not business growth, explains the revenue record.

HR and document control show the superintendent is 63, pension-eligible March 2028, successor 'TBD' since 2023, both assistants vacant, and no controlled dryer or blending procedure (E12). He confirms the practices are judgment-based, unshadowed, and that he plans to go part-time after 2027 (E13). The expansion plan relies on him for 2028 commissioning (E15). The claim is about dependency and documentation, not about whether his skill explains outcomes (that is R3).

The KPI workbook shows all non-maintenance cost per bushel moved only 14.6 to 14.5 cents while maintenance fell 2.8 to 1.9 cents, so essentially the whole 1.0-cent improvement is reduced maintenance spending against budget (E6). Over the same period the deferred backlog grew from $690K to $1.26M, with work orders explicitly deferred 'per cost review' (E7). The improvement is deferral, not efficiency. The GM's incentive rewards this KPI (E17), but the hypothesis does not depend on intent.

Trap: the 'goes in a drawer' comment and the uninvestigated near-miss look like silence. But near-miss reports rose from 6 to 9, all from front-line operators, and the July hazard was reported immediately (E8); 78% say they are comfortable reporting (E11). The failure is management response (19% see change, E11; closure without investigation, E8, E9), not withheld reports. The evidence counts against fear-driven silence.

The proposal is baselined on spike-inflated revenue (E15, E2) and prices are expected to return to about pre-rally levels (E16), so the proposal's case is unsound. But an unsound proposal does not show the project is non-viable: debt capacity depends on handling margin and net savings at normal prices, the cooperative earned $4.9M net savings at FY2025 prices (E2), and the proposal provides no margin or debt-service projection at any price (E15). Neither viability nor non-viability can be established; 'contradicted' overreaches.

Temporal order (program March 2025, record FY2026) is the only support. The auditor ties the $5.6M margin gain to price appreciation (E2); peers without any program improved net savings by a similar median 97% vs Cottonwood's 108% (E4), which rules the program out as the driver; and the program's only measured saving (~$0.3M) is a deferral of maintenance (E6, E7), not a real cost reduction; even with that $0.3M removed, FY2026 net savings ($9.9M) would still be a record, so the program is not what produced the record. The evidence counts against the link.

Mechanism: 91% of revenue is grain sales, i.e. price times volume (E2). Covariation with the rival ruled out: volume flat (E3) and handling revenue flat (E2), so the change is in price; prices rose 36-46% from February 2026 (E4), matching the timing in the auditor's note (E2). A cross-sectional comparison shows 22 peers with flat volume grew revenue by a similar amount (E4). This meets the causal standard.

His two sites do have lower shrink and discounts (E14), so the two co-occur. But the same two sites also have the only modern tower dryers (2019, 2021) versus 1998/2001 column dryers at the others, and there is no period in which his sites ran without him (E14). Equipment and person are perfectly confounded; causation is not established. This does not weaken H3, which concerns dependency, not attribution.

The deferred work order concerned the same bearing for high vibration and was deferred twice before it overheated (E7, E8), so the link is plausible and the two co-occur. But no investigation was done, the bearing was scrapped, and the Operations Manager names lubrication, belt rub, misalignment or age as live alternatives (E8, E9). The disconnected temperature sensor (E10) is a further unexamined factor. Mechanism is untested and rivals are open: association-only, not causal.

The expansion could be the right decision if viability at normal prices were shown (H6), but that is unknown: the proposal is baselined on FY2026 spike revenue, has no margin or debt-service analysis, and lacks staffing and maintenance plans (E15, E16). Committing $22.4M now is unjustified. It is not 'harmful' because nothing in the evidence shows the project itself would worsen outcomes; its merits are simply unestablished.

Independent inspection found critical dust, monitoring and baghouse hazards at Harlan Junction with a 2026-11-21 deadline (E10); 17 safety / dust-control work orders are deferred there (E7); staff say housekeeping is skipped (E11); and the policy-required investigation of an ignition-source near-miss was never done (E8). Restoring protective controls is justified regardless of any other open question.

The key-person dependency is established (H3: E12, E13) with a near deadline (part-time after the 2027 harvest, pension March 2028) and the expansion depends on him (E15). Capturing knowledge and naming a successor is valuable whether or not his practices explain the better shrink (R3 unresolved), so it does not wait on further evidence.

The 'gain' it would lock in is deferred maintenance (E6), the backlog has tripled with safety / dust-control items at Harlan (E7), the insurer has already flagged critical hazards there (E10), and the hiring freeze is what left the drying/grading succession and assistant posts empty (E12) and staff short for housekeeping (E11). Continuing both would worsen the documented hazards and key-person risk.

The vote rests on a revenue baseline the evidence shows is price-driven (E2, E4) with prices expected to fall back (E16), an unsourced throughput assumption against flat volume (E3, E15), missing staffing and maintenance plans, and reliance on a retiring superintendent (E12, E15). Deferring until the case is rebuilt directly addresses the unknown in H6 and is among the best next steps.

Evidence is sufficient to commit to substantive interventions now: safety remediation at Harlan Junction (independent inspection E10, backlog E7, uninvestigated near-miss E8) and drying/grading succession (E12, E13). It is not sufficient to approve the expansion, but sufficiency asks whether any substantive intervention is justified, and these are.
